title: NHTSA investigation into Tesla Autopilot crashes leads to a two-million-vehicle recall
description: Following a roughly two-year investigation into crashes involving Tesla's Autopilot driver-assist feature, including collisions with stationary emergency vehicles, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration found that Autopilot's driver-engagement controls could give drivers a false sense of security and were insufficient to prevent foreseeable misuse, identifying at least 13 fatal crashes where such misuse appeared to play a role. On 5 December 2023, Tesla agreed to a voluntary recall (NHTSA campaign 23V-838) covering roughly two million US vehicles, remedied via a free over-the-air software update that added visual alerts and could restrict Autosteer access after repeated driver misuse. NHTSA subsequently opened a follow-up investigation into whether the recall remedy was adequate.

history.note: Initial Phase 2A seed content, part of the Foundational Twenty. Exact vehicle count and fatal-crash figures are drawn from secondary reporting on the NHTSA investigation and recall report rather than a directly verified primary-document read; treat as approximate pending direct confirmation.

root_cause: NHTSA found Autopilot's system for ensuring driver engagement was inadequate, allowing foreseeable driver misuse — inattention or use outside intended operating conditions — to go uncorrected, contributing to crashes including some with stationary emergency vehicles.

relationships.reason: The same human-oversight and engagement-monitoring requirement addresses the gap NHTSA identified in Autopilot's driver-engagement controls.
This recall shows the same oversight gap at much larger fleet scale than the Uber incident.
